excerpt_i18n.en: Leiphone learned that on June 30, Yingzhi XBOT held the "2026 XBOT General-Purpose Catering Embodied Robot Launch" in Beijing. excerpt_i18n.en: Over the past year, almost everyone has been asking the same question: How much smarter can large AI models become? Agents, multimodal capabilities, and edge deployment have become the most talked-about narratives in the AI industry. But as AI enters physical carriers like glasses, cars, robots, and cameras, and begins interacting with humans on roads, in factories, and at home, we have discovered that a last mile still remains between the real world and large AI models. AI glasses need to recognize text in front of them, Robotaxis must assess surrounding road conditions, and robots have to decide their next move. They rely not only on algorithms but also on data such as images, speech, location, spatial relationships, device status, and environmental changes. This data must first be collected by terminals, then uploaded over the network, and processed by cloud or edge models. The model outputs also need to be returned to terminals via the network before they can be translated into real-world business actions. This places new pressure on mobile networks in the AI era. In the past, network fluctuations might have caused a video to buffer for a few seconds; in the future, the same fluctuations could lead to real-time recognition failures, remote control delays, or agents failing to complete actions. Mobile networks are no longer just simple content delivery channels. They need to identify connected objects, understand business types, assess real-time requirements, and decide which connections should be prioritized when resources are tight. The network of the physical AI era cannot be just a "wider pipe." The next wave of users of mobile networks will not only be humans.
excerpt_i18n.es: El año pasado, casi todos se hacían la misma pregunta: ¿qué tan inteligentes pueden volverse los grandes modelos de IA? Agentes, multimodalidad, despliegue en el borde conformaron la narrativa más vibrante de la industria de la IA. Pero cuando la IA empezó a integrarse en gafas, automóviles, robots, cámaras y otros soportes físicos, y a interactuar con humanos en carreteras, fábricas y hogares, descubrimos que aún queda un último kilómetro por recorrer entre el mundo real y los grandes modelos de IA. Las gafas de IA necesitan reconocer el texto que tienen delante, el Robotaxi debe evaluar las condiciones del tráfico circundante, el robot tiene que decidir el siguiente movimiento. No solo dependen de algoritmos, sino también de imagen, voz, posición, relaciones espaciales.

excerpt_i18n.en: In the past, creating highlight reels for football matches required editors to review footage, locate goals, celebrations, slow-motion replays, and audience reactions, then edit, package, add subtitles, and finally distribute to different platforms. The process was lengthy, labor-intensive, and relying on human experience and speed to capture traffic from hot moments. Now this workflow has been reorganized, with models and tool chains taking over the entire production process of match highlights. In the new workflow, AI can already understand the live stream in real time, identify signals such as camera switches, audio changes, player celebrations, referee whistles, quickly return highlight clips after key events, and generate independent slices ready for distribution. By the time a hot moment breaks, the video is already ready. The change behind this is not just that a certain tool has become more efficient, but that the production method of audio and video content is evolving from a human-driven workflow to an Agent-driven workflow. This not only involves calling models to generate and process audio and video content, but also forms new production tools and new production processes on this basis, truly approaching the ideal state of "creating a finished video with one sentence." This revolution in video production paradigm requires support from a new technical foundation. As Hang Mengyu, product leader of Volcano Engine AI Media Platform, shared at the 2026 Summer FORCE Conference Intelligent Video Cloud sub-forum, from "generating a segment of footage" to "delivering a finished video that can be launched, consumed, and distributed to audiences," there is still a whole set of professional audio and video processing work in between.
excerpt_i18n.es: Antes, para recopilar los momentos destacados de un partido de fútbol, los editores tenían que revisar el material, encontrar goles, celebraciones, repeticiones en cámara lenta y reacciones del público, luego cortar, empaquetar, añadir subtítulos y finalmente distribuir a diferentes plataformas. Un proceso largo y con mucha intervención manual. Aprovechar el tráfico de un momento viral dependía de la experiencia y la rapidez del editor. Ahora, este proceso se ha desglosado y reorganizado; los modelos y las cadenas de herramientas se encargan de todo el flujo de producción de vídeos destacados. En esta nueva cadena, la IA ya puede interpretar en tiempo real el flujo en directo, identificar cambios de plano, variaciones de audio, celebraciones de jugadores, silbidos del árbitro y otras señales, y devolver rápidamente fragmentos destacados justo después de que ocurran eventos clave, generando clips independientes listos para distribuir.
